records.name: CRUD-Only State Persistence
records.definition: Persisting only current state via create-read-update-delete, discarding the history that event sourcing preserves.

records.name: Direct Event Handler Calls
records.definition: Invoking event handlers by direct method call, coupling emitter to handler and defeating the event bus.

records.name: Direct Point-to-Point Calls
records.definition: Wiring services together with direct point-to-point calls, coupling each sender to specific receivers.

records.name: Duplicate Side Effects
records.definition: Reprocessing a message so its side effects run more than once, corrupting state when not idempotent.

records.name: Global ACID Transaction
records.definition: Attempting a single ACID transaction spanning multiple distributed services, creating tight coupling and availability loss.

records.name: Hidden Temporal Coupling
records.definition: An undocumented ordering requirement between operations that must run in a specific sequence to work correctly.

records.name: In-Memory Direct Invocation
records.definition: Calling a component directly in-process where a durable queue is needed, losing buffering and delivery guarantees.

records.name: In-Place Mutation
records.definition: Overwriting existing records in place where an append-only log is required, destroying history.

records.name: Infinite Redelivery Loop
records.definition: Endlessly redelivering a failing message with no dead-letter path, blocking the queue indefinitely.

records.name: Infrastructure Events in Domain
records.definition: Leaking infrastructure or technical events into the domain model, polluting it with concerns it should not hold.

records.name: Internal Domain Event Leakage
records.definition: Exposing internal domain events to external consumers, coupling them to private model details.

records.name: Irreversible Side Effects
records.definition: Performing side effects that cannot be undone within a workflow that may need to roll back.

records.name: Mutable State Only
records.definition: Keeping only mutable current state with no event record, so past states and changes cannot be recovered.

records.name: Point-to-Point Coupling
records.definition: Coupling a sender directly to a specific receiver, so adding a consumer requires changing the sender.

records.name: Shared Database

distinctFrom.reason: A shared database couples services through their data, while a cyclic deployment dependency couples them through their release order.

records.definition: Multiple services reading and writing one shared database, coupling them and destroying service autonomy.

records.name: Single Serial Consumer
records.definition: Processing a queue with one consumer in series, so throughput cannot scale with load.

records.name: Unified CRUD Model
records.definition: Using one shared model for both reads and writes, preventing each from being optimized for its purpose.

records.name: Broker/Event Bus
records.definition: A runtime intermediary that routes messages between publishers and subscribers.

records.name: Command/Query Separation
records.definition: Separating operations that change state from those that return data, so each method has a single purpose.

records.name: Consumer
records.definition: A component that receives and processes messages from a queue or topic.

records.name: Deduplication Key
records.definition: A stable identifier attached to a message that lets a consumer detect and drop duplicates.

records.name: Event Contract
records.definition: The agreed schema and semantics of an event that publishers and subscribers both honor.

records.name: Event Schema
records.definition: A formal definition of the structure and fields of an event's payload.

records.name: Event Semantics
records.definition: The agreed meaning of what an event represents and the conditions under which it is emitted.

records.name: Events
records.definition: Records of things that have happened in a system, emitted for other components to react to.

records.name: Immutable Events
records.definition: The requirement that recorded events never change once written, only be appended to.

records.name: Local Transaction
records.definition: A transaction confined to a single service's own datastore, the atomic unit a saga or outbox composes.

records.name: Message Relay
records.definition: A component that reads pending messages from an outbox and publishes them to the broker.

records.name: Ordered Log

distinctFrom.reason: An ordered log keeps records in write order, while an event schema defines what each record holds.

records.definition: An append-only sequence of records that preserves the order in which they were written.

records.name: Own Data
records.definition: The requirement that each service alone own and control its data store.

records.name: Publisher

distinctFrom.reason: A publisher emits messages, while the broker routes them between publishers and subscribers.
A publisher sends to a topic, while a subscriber receives from it.

records.definition: A component that emits messages to a topic or bus for subscribers to receive.

records.name: Reconciliation
records.definition: The activity of detecting and resolving divergence between replicas so they converge to a consistent state.

records.name: Reversible/Compensable Step
records.definition: The requirement that each step in a distributed workflow can be undone by a compensating action.

records.name: Routing
records.definition: The ability to direct each message to its correct destination based on topic, key, or rule.

records.name: Subscriber

distinctFrom.reason: A subscriber receives a topic's messages, while the broker routes them to it.

records.definition: A component that registers interest in a topic and receives its messages.

records.name: Subscriber Model
records.definition: A representation of which consumers subscribe to which topics and how they receive messages.

records.name: User Expectations
records.definition: The behavior users assume a system will exhibit, such as seeing their own writes immediately.

records.name: Asynchronous Processing
records.definition: The ability to handle work without blocking the caller, decoupling request from completion.

records.name: Atomic State Change + Message Publish
records.definition: The ability to commit a state change and publish its corresponding message as one atomic unit.

records.name: Consumer Elasticity
records.definition: The ability to add or remove consumers dynamically to match message volume.

records.name: Cross-Service Communication
records.definition: The ability for independent services to exchange information without direct coupling.

records.name: Decoupled Domain Reactions
records.definition: The ability for domain logic to react to events without the emitter knowing its consumers.

records.name: Decoupled Event Distribution
records.definition: The ability to distribute events to many consumers without the source depending on any of them.

records.name: Distributed Autonomy
records.definition: The ability for distributed nodes to operate and decide independently without central coordination.

records.name: Failure Recovery
records.definition: The ability to restore correct operation after a failure through compensation or retry.

records.name: Fan-Out Notification
records.definition: The ability to deliver one event to many interested subscribers at once.

records.name: Long-Running Transactions
records.definition: The ability to carry a business transaction across many steps and a long duration via compensation.

records.name: Parallel Message Processing

distinctFrom.reason: Parallel message processing is several consumers working at once, while consumer elasticity is changing how many there are to match volume.

records.definition: The ability for multiple consumers to process messages from the same source at once.

records.name: Poison-Message Quarantine

distinctFrom.reason: Quarantine moves a failing message aside, while reprocessing after the fix sends it through again.

records.definition: The ability to divert a repeatedly-failing message to a separate queue so it stops blocking others.

records.name: Read/Write Model Optimization
records.definition: The ability to shape read and write models independently for their differing access patterns.

records.name: Reprocessing After Fix
records.definition: The ability to reprocess quarantined messages once the underlying defect is fixed.

records.name: Safe Message Redelivery
records.definition: The ability to redeliver a message without causing duplicate effects, given idempotent handling.

records.name: Temporal Modeling
records.definition: The ability to model how state evolved over time by preserving each change as an event.

records.name: Temporal Queries
records.definition: The ability to ask what a system's state was at any past point in time.

records.name: Work Distribution
records.definition: The ability to spread units of work across many workers via a broker.

records.name: At-Least-Once Delivery Safety
records.definition: The degree to which a message is guaranteed to be delivered at least once, tolerating duplicates.

records.name: Event Reliability
records.definition: The degree to which events are guaranteed to be delivered despite failures.

records.name: Business Complexity
records.definition: The degree of domain intricacy that a coordination mechanism must accommodate.

records.name: Delivery Ordering
records.definition: The degree to which messages are delivered in a defined order, which broad fan-out can weaken.

records.name: Duplication with Domain Events
records.definition: The degree of overlap between integration events and domain events that must be kept in sync.

records.name: Event Granularity
records.definition: The degree of coarseness or fineness at which events are defined, trading detail against volume.

records.name: Event Storm / Traceability
records.definition: The degree to which a high volume of events makes end-to-end flows hard to trace.

records.name: Global Consistency
records.definition: The degree to which all nodes reflect the same state at once, which service autonomy gives up.

records.name: Immediate Consistency
records.definition: The degree to which a read reflects the latest write instantly, which asynchronous processing defers.

records.name: Operational Dependency
records.definition: The degree to which a system's operation depends on a message broker remaining available.

records.name: Query Complexity
records.definition: The degree of difficulty of answering queries when state is stored as an event history rather than current rows.

records.name: Relay Complexity
records.definition: The degree of added complexity of running a relay process that forwards messages from an outbox.

records.name: State Overhead
records.definition: The degree of extra state a consumer must retain to deduplicate or order messages.

records.name: Storage Growth
records.definition: The degree to which an append-only log's storage footprint grows unbounded over time.

records.name: Storage Volume
records.definition: The degree to which retaining a full event stream consumes large amounts of storage.

records.name: Strong Consistency
records.definition: The degree to which all reads see the latest write, which event-driven asynchrony relaxes.

records.name: Strong Immediate Consistency
records.definition: The degree to which every read reflects the most recent write without delay, which eventual consistency relaxes.

records.name: Workflow Complexity
records.definition: The degree of intricacy of coordinating a multi-step distributed workflow.

records.name: Query Projection
records.definition: A technique for maintaining a read model shaped for one query, updated from the writes it depends on.

records.name: Introduce Async Event
records.definition: A technique for replacing a synchronous call that need not complete in the request with an event a consumer handles later.

records.name: Own Data per Service
records.definition: A technique for giving each service its own store and letting others reach the data only through its contract.

records.name: Offset Tracking
records.definition: A technique for recording how far each consumer has read in a stream, so it resumes there and can replay from earlier.

records.name: Snapshot Compaction
records.definition: A technique for periodically storing a snapshot of state derived from a log, so readers replay only the events after it.

records.name: Non-Replayable Processing
records.definition: A defect in which consumed events cannot be read again, so a consumer cannot rebuild its state or recover from a fault.
